Part 1

Water below the ground

The unsaturated and saturated zones, and why soil water matters

Two zones below the surface

Key idea

Water beneath the surface is in two zones: the unsaturated zone (soil water) and the saturated zone (groundwater).

  • The unsaturated zone, also called the zone of aeration, includes the soil water zone
  • The zone of saturation contains groundwater

This lecture and course

We focus on water in the unsaturated (vadose) zone: soil water or pore water.

Groundwater is a huge topic of its own and is not covered in this course. Although it is in book chapter 5, please read chapter 6 instead. If you are interested, take CE 4/569: Subsurface Hydrology.

Soil water: why do we care?

Key idea

Soil water links rainfall to crops, floods, droughts and contaminants: almost every hydrology question passes through the soil.

  1. Drought mitigation
  2. Water contaminant movement
  3. Agriculture
  4. Flood prevention
  5. The hydrologic cycle as a whole

Think about it

How much rain becomes runoff (floods) versus soil storage (crops, drought buffer) is decided in the top meter or two of soil.

Water storage below ground

Key idea

The water table separates the unsaturated zone above from the saturated zone below.

  • Unsaturated zone: soil water (vadose zone)
  • Saturated zone: groundwater (phreatic zone)

Read the figure

Where the water table meets the land surface, groundwater feeds surface water such as a stream.

Unsaturated zone definitions

Key idea

Water enters the soil by infiltration; how fast it can do so is the infiltration capacity.

  • Infiltration: the process of water entering the soil
  • Infiltration rate: the volume flux of water entering the soil, per unit area per unit time
  • Infiltration capacity: the maximum rate infiltration can occur under specific moisture conditions
  • Vadose zone: the unsaturated zone, from the ground surface down to the water table. Vadose means “shallow” in Latin

Read the sketch

Once in the soil, water redistributes, is taken up by plants, moves sideways as interflow, rises by capillarity or recharges the water table.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 What is the difference between infiltration rate and infiltration capacity?

The rate is how fast water is actually entering the soil. The capacity is the maximum rate possible under the current moisture conditions.

Q2 Which zone is the vadose zone, and where are its upper and lower boundaries?

The unsaturated zone, from the ground surface down to the water table.

Part 2

Pores and water content

The three phases of soil, and the numbers we use to describe them

Pores (or voids)

Key idea

Pores are the open spaces between soil particles and organic matter. They hold the air and water in soil.

Read the left figure

Pore size follows particle size: large pores between large particles, tiny pores between clay particles.

Read the right figure

Above the water table pores hold air and water; below it they are full of water. The capillary fringe sits just above the water table.

Unsaturated vs. saturated pores

Key idea

The water table divides the zone of aeration (pores partly filled) from the zone of saturation (pores completely filled).

During high rainfall, pore spaces can fill with water.

  • Saturation zone: all the pores are filled with water
  • Aeration zone: pores are partially filled, with water between particles and organic matter

The aeration zone has three sub-zones

  1. Soil water zone
  2. Intermediate zone
  3. Capillary fringe

A soil sample’s three phases

Key idea

We model a soil sample as three phases stacked in a column: gas, water and solids.

  • Vt: total volume
  • Vg: volume of gas (soil air)
  • Vw: volume of water
  • Vp: volume of pores = Vg + Vw
  • Vs: volume of soil solids (particles)

Every water content and density on the next slides is a ratio of these volumes or masses.

Three ways to express soil water content

Key idea

Soil water content can be volumetric (θ), gravimetric (G) or saturated (n). Do not mix them up: θ ≠ G.

Volumetric water content (θv)

θv = Vw / Vt = (Mwet − Mdry) / (ρw Vt)

Volume of water over total sample volume; ρw = density of water.

Gravimetric water content (G)

G = (Mwet − Mdry) / Mdry

Weight of water over weight of dry soil.

Saturated water content (n)

The maximum water a soil can hold, which equals its porosity.

Example 1: water content

Key idea

A wetland sample weighs 1450 g wet and 1225 g oven-dry, with a total volume of 1115 cm³. Find G and θv (ρw = 1 g/cm³).

Mass of water

1450 g − 1225 g = 225 g

Volumetric water content

θv = 225 g / (1 g/cm³ × 1115 cm³) = 0.202

Gravimetric water content

G = 225 g / 1225 g = 0.183

θ and G differ because one divides by volume and the other by dry mass.

Porosity, bulk density and saturation

Key idea

Porosity is the share of soil that is open space; bulk density is dry mass per total volume; saturation is how full the pores are.

Porosity (n)

n = Vp / Vt = 1 − Vs / Vt = 1 − ρb / ρm

ρm is particle density, about 2650 kg/m³ (= Md / Vs).

Dry bulk density (ρb)

ρb = Md / Vt

Degree of saturation (S): wetness

S = Vw / Vp = θ / n

Example 2: bulk density

Key idea

The soil’s aluminosilicate particles have ρm = 2.6 g/cm³. If the porosity is n = 0.5, what is the bulk density ρb?

Start from porosity

n = 1 − ρb / ρm

0.5 = 1 − ρb / 2.6 g/cm³

Solve

ρb = (1 − 0.5) × 2.6 = 1.3 g/cm³

Answer: 1.3 g/cm³. Half the volume is pores, so the bulk density is half the particle density.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q3 A 100 cm³ core weighs 165 g wet and 140 g dry. Find θv and G.

Water = 25 g. θv = 25 / 100 = 0.25; G = 25 / 140 = 0.18.

Q4 A soil has a porosity of 0.40 and θ = 0.30. What is its degree of saturation?

S = θ / n = 0.30 / 0.40 = 0.75 (75% of the pores are full).

Q5 Using ρm = 2.65 g/cm³, what is the porosity of a soil with ρb = 1.59 g/cm³?

n = 1 − 1.59 / 2.65 = 1 − 0.60 = 0.40.

Part 3

Tension and capillarity

Adhesion, cohesion and capillary rise

Adhesion and cohesion

Key idea

Surface tension forces in soil come from adhesion (water to solids) and cohesion (water to water).

  • Adhesion: the attraction of water to the sides of the pore (water to solids)
  • Cohesion: the attraction of water to water

Try it

Water droplets are flatter on the hibiscus flower than on the grass. What is causing it, adhesion or cohesion? (Answer in the check questions.)

Polarity and hydrogen bonding

Key idea

Cohesion and adhesion result from water’s polarity and hydrogen bonding.

Read the left figure

Cohesion: water molecules attracted to each other. Adhesion: water attracted to solids such as clay minerals.

Read the right figure

Water in contact with the soil matrix has a lower free energy. Tension is greater close to the particle (lower energy) than at the outside of the film (higher energy).

Hydrogen bonds prevent

  • Free drainage of water from small pores
  • Removal of water by evaporation

Capillary fringe

Key idea

Capillarity is caused by adhesion of water to a surface. It lifts water against gravity: the smaller the pore, the higher the rise.

H = 0.15 / r

Capillary rise H (cm) for a pore of radius r (cm).

The capillary fringe is the layer where groundwater seeps up from the water table by capillary action to fill pores. Pores at its base are full due to tension saturation.

How thick is the saturated part?

  • Less than the full capillary rise, because pore sizes are mixed
  • Small, uniform pores: soil can be saturated for several feet above the water table
  • Large pores: only a few inches

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 Droplets are flatter on the hibiscus flower than on grass. Is that adhesion or cohesion?

Adhesion: the water is attracted to the flower surface and spreads out. On the grass, cohesion wins and the water beads up.

Q7 Using H = 0.15/r, how high does water rise in a pore of radius 0.005 cm? In a pore of radius 0.05 cm?

0.15 / 0.005 = 30 cm; 0.15 / 0.05 = 3 cm. Ten times smaller pore, ten times higher rise.

Q8 Why is the capillary fringe thicker in a fine, uniform soil than in a coarse gravel?

Fine soils have small pores, and capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore radius. Gravel has large pores, so water rises only a few inches.

Part 4

Suction, retention and hysteresis

How tightly soil holds water, and why wetting and drying differ

Soil suction (soil moisture tension)

Key idea

Soil suction is a negative pressure created by the interaction of soil, water and air in the pores.

  • It depends on the strength of the capillary force
  • It depends on the amount of water and the pore size distribution
  • The relationship is the suction–moisture curve
  • Hysteresis: the water content at a given suction depends on whether the soil is wetting or drying

Read the graph

At the same suction, Yolo clay holds much more water than Plainfield sand. Note how non-linear the curves are.

Water retention in a heterogeneous profile

Key idea

In a real soil, pore sizes vary with depth, so the water held (r1, r2, r3) is different at each level of the profile.

Read the figure

Water rises from the water table through a pore that narrows and widens. Each meniscus has a different radius: r1, r2 and r3.

Smaller radius → stronger capillary pull. That is why the water held changes up the profile, and why the contact angle between water and soil matters.

Hysteresis during drying and wetting

Key idea

Hysteresis: the value of a property lags behind changes in the effect causing it. Soil holds more water while drying than while wetting, at the same suction.

Read the graph

At the same pressure head (suction), the boundary drying curve sits above the boundary wetting curve.

So there is a different relationship between soil water and soil suction during wetting and drying.

Why?

Narrow pore necks stop pores from draining until suction is high, and trapped air keeps pores from filling completely when wetting.

Moisture-holding forces

Key idea

Soil holds water with two forces: absorptive and capillary.

  1. Absorptive forces: clays absorb water into their crystalline structure, causing expansion
  2. Capillary forces: water held in pores by adhesion and cohesion

Read the figures

Polar water molecules push between the clay plates when wet (right). When the clay dries, it shrinks and cracks (left).

Soil components

Key idea

Soil is a mix of solids, living material, water and air, and the water sits in the spaces they leave.

  • A skeleton of coarser materials
  • Clays
  • An assortment of living and dead biotic material
  • Water and air

Read the figure

Water forms films on soil particles and fills small pores; air fills the larger ones; a root grows through the pore space.

Tension draws water into the soil

Key idea

Tension between soil and water draws moisture into dry soil. As the soil wets up and capillary forces weaken, infiltration capacity decreases.

Read the graph

Infiltration capacity (curve) starts high and declines through the storm. When rainfall rises above the curve, the excess becomes surface runoff.

This is the link to the next two lectures: infiltration (5e) and runoff (5f).

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q9 At the same suction, a drying soil holds more water than a wetting soil. What is this called?

Hysteresis.

Q10 Why does infiltration capacity decline during a long storm?

As the soil fills with water, the capillary (tension) forces that pull water in diminish, so the soil accepts water more slowly.

Q11 Which force makes a clay soil swell when wet?

Absorptive force: clays absorb water into their crystalline structure.
